**Lufthansa Flight 2904 — the aeroplane was on the ground; the computer disagreed (1993)**

On 14 September 1993 an Airbus A320 flying from Frankfurt landed at Warsaw in heavy rain, ran off the end of the runway and struck an earth embankment. Two of the seventy people on board were killed and more than fifty injured.

The braking systems had not worked when the crew wanted them — not because they failed, but because the software had been told precisely what "on the ground" means and was not yet satisfied. Ground spoilers and thrust reversers required a compression load of at least 6.3 tonnes on *each* main landing gear; the wheel brakes required the wheels to be spinning faster than 72 knots. Each is a conjunction: this AND that, or nothing happens.

Both conditions failed at once. Expecting a crosswind, the crew landed with one wing low, so the right gear took the weight and the left did not — "both struts loaded" stayed false. The runway was flooded, so the wheels aquaplaned rather than spinning up, and the 72-knot test stayed false too. Roughly nine seconds passed between first touchdown and the spoilers deploying. Each condition alone is a sensible test for being on the ground. Chained by AND, they described a landing that had not happened.

That is what a truth table is for. An implication makes no claim at all when its premise is false: it sits there, vacuously true, while you assume it is protecting you. Writing the preconditions of an action in a planner, or the domain of a variable in a constraint problem, is the same commitment these engineers made — whatever you have not written down, the system will not do. Enumerate the cases before you trust the rule.

**Grand Forks — a flood forecast that had error bars nobody was shown (1997)**

Through the spring of 1997 the US National Weather Service told Grand Forks, North Dakota and East Grand Forks, Minnesota that the Red River would crest at around 49 feet. The towns prepared for 49 feet. On 22 April the river crested above 54 feet, overwhelmed the dykes and flooded both communities; Roger Pielke Jr's study of the event puts the damage at one to two billion dollars.

The forecast was not a lie. It was a single number pulled out of a distribution, and the distribution never reached the people deciding what to build. In *The Signal and the Noise*, Nate Silver reports the forecast carried a margin of error of roughly plus or minus nine feet, against flood protection standing at about 51 feet. A 54-foot crest was well inside the range the forecasters' own models allowed — it was not a surprise to the mathematics, only to the audience.

Pielke found the service attached uncertainty as a qualitative disclaimer at the foot of a confidently quantitative product. Officials who read the same forecast privately assumed error bars of anywhere between one and six feet. Everyone was working with a probability distribution; each had silently replaced it with a different guess.

This is the habit the lesson is training. A probability is a statement about a spread of outcomes, and an expected value is the average of that spread, not a prediction of what will happen. When you compute a posterior with Bayes' rule or an expected reward for an action, you get a number — and the number is only half the answer. Carry the uncertainty with it, and say out loud how wrong it could be.

**NATS — two waypoints with the same name, four thousand miles apart (2023)**

On the morning of 28 August 2023 the software that receives flight plans for UK airspace stopped, and stayed down for some seven hours. More than 1,500 flights were cancelled. The Civil Aviation Authority's review put the number of passengers affected at over 700,000.

A flight plan is a path through a graph. The nodes are waypoints — named points in the sky — and the plan lists them in order. NATS's flight plan processing system wants only the British part of that path, so it looks for the node where the route enters UK airspace and the node where it leaves, and extracts the sub-path between them. That morning a plan arrived carrying two waypoints that shared a designator: one near the beginning of the route, one near the end, some 4,000 nautical miles apart, both outside UK airspace. Duplicate waypoint names exist worldwide; the standards ask only that identical designators be kept far apart, which these were.

The system found the entry point, then matched the exit designator to the wrong one of the pair. Asked for the stretch of route between them, it could not produce anything valid, raised a critical exception and stopped. The backup, given the same plan and running the same code, stopped the same way.

This lesson says a graph is nodes joined by edges, and that a node's neighbours are found by looking its name up in an adjacency list. Read that as a promise you have to keep: identity must be unique, or a path through the graph is not well defined. When you key an adjacency list by name, or drop a state into a visited set, ask what happens when two different things answer to the same key.

**GTA Online — six minutes of loading, hiding in one quadratic loop (2021)**

For years, players of Rockstar Games' GTA Online complained that the game took around six minutes to reach the menu on machines that ran everything else instantly. In 2021 a developer publishing as t0st profiled the running game and wrote up what they found. Rockstar shipped the fix in an update, credited t0st by name, and — as widely reported — paid a $10,000 bug bounty.

The profile was strange. Disk idle. Network idle. Graphics card idle. One CPU core pinned at 100 per cent for four minutes. The work was a 10 MB text file listing about 63,000 purchasable items, and two routines were grinding through it. The parser used a C library function that re-measures the length of the entire remaining text every time it reads one value, so reading n values costs on the order of n²/2 scans. Then every parsed item was compared against every item already stored, to reject duplicates that could not occur — t0st counted roughly 1.98 billion comparisons.

Neither routine was wrong. On a hundred items nobody would ever notice. The defect was not in what the code did but in how its cost grew with n, and no amount of faster hardware was going to rescue it.

Big-O is the notation for precisely that. O(n) and O(n²) behave identically on your test data and diverge violently on real data, which is why you rank growth rates rather than time a stopwatch. Hold on to that when you reach uninformed search: b^d is not a warning about slow code, it is a statement that the machine will never finish. Estimating the growth rate before you run anything is the skill.

**The Willoughby–Hoye scripts — same code, same data, a different answer per computer (2019)**

In 2019 a group at the University of Hawaii at Manoa, led by Jayanti Bhandari Neupane and Philip Williams, ran a widely used pair of Python scripts that chemists rely on to compare predicted and measured NMR data. Running the same inputs on four machines gave three different answers: as reported in *Organic Letters* and covered by The Register, macOS Mavericks and Windows 10 produced one value, Ubuntu 16 and macOS Mojave produced two others.

The cause was one line. The scripts gathered their input files with Python's `glob.glob()`, then paired the two kinds of file up by position. `glob` returns filenames in whatever order the operating system hands them over — it does not sort. On one system the pairing lined up; on another it did not, and the calculation quietly used mismatched data. The Register reported that the scripts had been cited in more than 150 published papers. The repair was a single call to `.sort()`.

Nothing here was exotic. The authors had made an assumption about ordering that Python never promised, and because the code ran on one machine it looked correct.

This is why the lesson ends with environments and version control rather than more syntax. A `requirements.txt`, a pinned virtual environment and a repository someone else can clone are what let a second person get your number — or fail to, visibly, instead of silently. And when you reach for a Python container, know what it guarantees: a `set` has no order at all, a `dict` key must be hashable, and `glob` gives you an order you did not choose.
